title: ICL and PDL: describing and operating instruments
summary: IEEE 1687 comes with two languages. **ICL** describes the hardware — registers, ports, SIBs, muxes and how they connect. **PDL** describes how an instrument is used, at the instrument's own level. A **retargeting** tool combines both and produces the chip-level JTAG operations.
objectives: Read a small ICL description of an instrument and a SIB.
Use the main PDL commands: iProc, iWrite, iRead, iApply, iRunLoop, iCall, iMerge.
Explain how iApply merges many requests into few scans.
Explain retargeting and why PDL stays portable.

blocks.md: ICL (Instrument Connectivity Language) describes **modules** and how they are connected. A module lists its **ports** (the scan interface of Topic 6 and data ports), its **registers** and **muxes**, and the **instances** of other modules inside it.

blocks.caption: Main ICL keywords

blocks.title: Who writes ICL?
blocks.md: Instrument designers write the ICL of their instrument; the DFT tool that inserts the network writes the ICL of the network and the chip. Nobody writes the chip-level ICL by hand.

PDL (Procedural Description Language) is written from the **instrument's point of view**: write this field, wait, read that field. It knows nothing about the network around the instrument. PDL comes in two levels: **level 0**, a fixed list of commands, and **level 1**, which adds the full Tcl language — loops, conditions, and reading back data with *iGetReadData* to decide what to do next.

rows: the following procedures belong to module *m*
queue a write to a register, field or data port
queue a read and the value expected
execute all queued writes and reads in as few scans as possible
wait *n* clocks (e.g. while a BIST runs)
call a procedure of an instrument further down the hierarchy
run the iCalls in between concurrently, sharing scans
state that a clock must be running for the following operations
blocks.caption: Main PDL commands (level 0)

blocks.code:
iProcsForModule mbist_tdr

iProc run_test {algo} {
  iWrite config $algo
  iWrite start  1
  iApply
  iRunLoop 1100000 -tck
  iRead  done 1
  iRead  pass 1
  iApply
}

subsections.title: iApply: few scans for many requests

steps.title: Queue
steps.md: iWrite and iRead only **queue** requests. They can address different instruments.

steps.title: Build the path
steps.md: At **iApply** the tool finds a path through the network that contains all addressed registers, and the SIB settings to open it.

steps.title: One scan
steps.md: One DR scan writes both start bits and checks the sensor. Registers on the path that were not addressed keep their values.

blocks.title: iMerge: instruments in parallel
blocks.md: Inside **iMerge**, the iCalls to several instruments are interleaved: their iApply steps are combined into shared scans. Starting 40 MBIST controllers then costs about the same number of scans as starting one.

blocks.caption: Instrument-level PDL plus the network's ICL become chip-level JTAG operations

blocks.md: The **retargeting** tool reads the PDL of every instrument and the ICL of the whole chip. For every iApply it computes which SIBs and muxes must be set, how many scans are needed, and which bits to shift — and writes the result as tester patterns (or as software for on-chip access).

blocks.code:
# chip-level PDL: call instrument procedures by instance path
iProcsForModule chip
iProc test_all_mbist {} {
  iMerge -begin
    iCall coreA.mbist1.run_test MarchCminus
    iCall coreA.mbist2.run_test MarchCminus
  iMerge -end
}

blocks.title: Write once, reuse everywhere
blocks.md: When an instrument moves to a new chip, its ICL and PDL stay the same. Only the network around it — and its ICL — changes, and retargeting produces the new patterns automatically.
